# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–14 (Complete – Updated 115)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Early morning of Waterloo campaign battle day in Brussels—Regiment receives marching orders; troops march within hours. French crossed Sambre; British left already engaged. Bugle from Place of Arms signals at dawn; whole city awakens to drums and pipes. Regiment departs in early morning.**
- **Earlier Timeline**: Spring of fourth year with Seena Orlwood drowned; Winter of third year with frost; Evening at Brighton; Fine moonlight night of May; Army ordered to Belgium; Transports to Ostend; Amelia and Jos to Ramsgate; Belgium in happy season transitioning to war; Famous Brussels ball evening of 15 June 1815 (historical).
- **Primary Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers), Brighton, Mirecombe, Wilhaven, Chatham, Harwich, Fulham, Ramsgate, Ostend, Brussels (Hotel de Ville, Park, Hotel du Parc, opera-house, restaurateur's, Place of Arms), Belgium.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Actions - Departure Morning**: Came to Jos's quarters at dawn before regiment's departure (while George occupied with own affairs and grief at parting). Roused Jos from sleep; insisted on shaking hands before departure. Instructed Jos with utmost seriousness: "We march in a quarter of an hour, Sedley, and neither George nor I may ever come back. You are not to stir from this town until you ascertain how things go. Stay here and watch over your sister, and comfort her, and see that no harm comes to her. If anything happens to George, remember she has no one but you in the world to look to. If it goes wrong with the army, you'll see her safe back to England; you will promise me on your word that you will never desert her. I know you won't." Asked if Jos needed gold to return to England in case of misfortune. (Dobbin appeared hypocrite, listening intently toward George's apartments, striding about, upsetting chairs, beating tattoo, biting nails—showing great inward emotion—while professing tender interest in Jos.)
- **Earlier Actions**: At play-table during ball aftermath, whispered to George: "The enemy has passed the Sambre, and our left is already engaged. Come away. We are to march in three hours." George responded with wild hurray. Arrived Brighton via Slaughters' hotel; dined with officers; assumed jovial manner hiding feelings. In George's room: delivered disinheritance letter; George erupted; Dobbin offered financial support. At Chatham: wore shells on frockcoat, crimson sash and sabre; recognized Amelia; never spoke during Mrs. O'Dowd's party; took Jos home (maudlin); handed Amelia into carriage (she rebuked him smilingly); loitered smoking cigar watching George's windows; bought piano for Amelia's father's house at Fulham. In Belgium: "In a rage" at treatment of Amelia by Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Countess of Bareacres; accompanied Jos and Amelia on carriage drives; at opera shrieked with laughter when Rebecca kissed fingers, again when Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment; Rebecca leaned on his arm returning to her box. Few days after opera: remonstrated with George about giving up play. At famous Brussels ball: only person who disturbed Amelia's unhappy thoughts; brought refreshments, sat beside her; when Amelia clung to him (called him by Christian name), she begged him to take her home; he went away with her quickly through crowds.
- **Internal Conflict**: Deeply troubled by guilt over hastening marriage. Secret adoration of Amelia is his "greatest privilege and hope of life"; privately resolved he would not have let her go to Belgium if married to her. Knows Amelia considers him plain, awkward, ungainly. Now avoided by George in public.
- **Reputation**: "Greatly respected in the regiment, as the best officer and the cleverest man in it"

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Actions - Final Hours**: At play-table during ball aftermath, won repeatedly; said "Everything succeeds with me to-night"; restlessness persisted; drank many bumpers of wine. Upon Dobbin's news, gave wild hurray, clapped glass on table, walked away speedily. Nerves quivered with excitement at long-looked-for news; thought about thousand things—past life, future chances, fate before him, wife, child perhaps from whom unseen he might part. Wished night's work undone and could say farewell to tender and guileless being by whose love he had set such little store. Thought over brief married life; in few weeks had frightfully dissipated little capital; had been wild and reckless. If mischance befall him, what left for her? How unworthy he was. Remembered father's generosity. Sat down and wrote farewell letter to father (remembering duel engagement letter reference). Dawn streaked sky as he closed letter; sealed and kissed superscription; thought how he deserted generous father and thousand kindnesses. **Had looked into Amelia's bedroom when entered; she lay quiet with eyes seemed closed; he was glad she was asleep. Upon arriving at quarters from ball, found regimental servant already making departure preparations (arrangements made quickly and silently). Debated whether to wake Amelia or leave note for Jos. Went in to look at her once again. She had been awake when he first entered but kept eyes closed so wakefulness should not seem to reproach him. When he returned after herself, her timid heart felt more at ease; she turned towards him, fell into light sleep. George came in and looked again, entering more softly. By pale night-lamp could see her sweet pale face—purple eyelids fringed and closed; one round arm smooth and white lay outside coverlet. He saw how pure, gentle, tender, friendless she was; how selfish, brutal, black with crime he was. Heart-stained and shame-stricken, stood at bed's foot. Came to bedside, looked at little soft hand; bent over pillow noiselessly toward gentle pale face. Two fair arms closed tenderly round his neck as he stooped down. "I am awake, George," the poor child said, with a sob fit to break the little heart nestled so closely by his own. At that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums of infantry and shrill pipes of Scotch, whole city awoke.** (George departed with regiment at dawn; left Amelia at that tender embrace interrupted by bugle signal.)
- **Earlier Status**: Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited (determination "final and irrevocable"). Receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Lost £140 to Rawdon at cards; obtained £2,000 cheque from Hulker and Bullock bankers. At Chatham: sent Amelia to mother with carte blanche; paid for everything requisite. At Brussels: ashamed of regiment, resolved to exchange to better regiment soon; takes wife to nightly jaunts; quite pleased with himself. Danced with Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Rebecca at ball. Called upon ladies; rode in Park; asked their party to dinner at restaurateur's. Purchased horse for private riding. Told Amelia Rebecca is comfort to "get rid of this damn'd Irishwoman" (Mrs. O'Dowd). **Carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she not deceived); consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." At opera: claimed "We bear the same arms" to General Tufto; Rebecca left his box giving "queerest, knowingest look." After opera: Dobbin criticized Rebecca; George defended her. Few days after opera: told Dobbin "we play low; I won last night" and suggested Crawley does not cheat; plays repeatedly with Crawley now. General Tufto dines abroad almost constantly; George always welcome in Crawley's apartments.**

**Amelia Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Moment - Departure**: When George bent over her pillow at bedside in early morning, two fair arms closed tenderly round his neck as he stooped down. "I am awake, George," the poor child said, with a sob fit to break the little heart nestled so closely by his own. At that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums and pipes, whole city awoke. George departed with regiment; Amelia left at bedside as city awakens to battle.
- **Earlier Status**: Troubled by Rebecca's wit and misgivings about her. Rose early at Chatham; packed trunks with "greatest alacrity" while George lay in bed. Mother clasped her to heart with "all maternal eagerness and affection." Knelt seeking spiritual consolation. Bustling about completing outfit with great taste and elegant discernment. Adopted by regiment with acclamation. **In Belgium**: natural and unaffected; only amused by Mrs. O'Dowd's eccentricities. Letters home filled with delight and gratitude. Husband bade her buy laces, millinery, jewels; he kindest, best, most generous of men. At general's party: Countess of Bareacres would not answer; Lady Blanche stared with eye-glass; Amelia wrote piteous accounts home. At opera: gentle eyes fixed anxiously on Rebecca and George; embraced Rebecca with affectionate rapture. When visited Rawdon and Rebecca's quarters: displayed evident unwillingness and high and mighty manner; George scolded her violently; she silent but more bashful and awkward on second visit. Not quite six weeks married. Aware George carrying on flirtation with Rebecca; does not plague him with jealousy but becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. At Brussels ball: did not know soul; sat quite unnoticed in corner except when Rawdon came and Dobbin brought refreshments. Alarmed by Rebecca telling her George would go on playing. Witnessing Rebecca's request to George for scarf and flowers proved "quite too much for her"; suddenly clinging to Dobbin called him by Christian name, begging him to take her home; went away with him quickly through crowds; did not sleep that night.

**Captain Rawdon Crawley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Departure Actions**: Upon receiving final news that campaign was opened and troops to march, gravity became such that Rebecca rallied him, which hurt his feelings. Said with tremor in voice: "You don't suppose I'm afraid, Becky, I should think. But I'm a pretty good mark for a shot, and you see if it brings me down, why I leave one and perhaps two behind me whom I should wish to provide for, as I brought 'em into the scrape. It is no laughing matter that, Mrs. C., anyways." This showed genuine concern—previously had seldom thought about anything but himself until last few months when Love obtained mastery over dragoon. **Made last dispositions: went through various items of little catalogue of effects, striving to see how they might be turned into money for Rebecca's benefit in case any accident should befall him. Pleased himself by noting down with pencil in big schoolboy handwriting various items of portable property which might be sold for widow's advantage, for example: "My double-barril by Manton, say 40 guineas; my driving cloak, lined with sable fur, 50 pounds; my duelling pistols in rosewood case (same which I shot Captain Marker), 20 pounds; my regulation saddle-holsters and housings; my Laurie ditto," and so forth, over all of which articles he made Rebecca the mistress. Dressed himself in oldest and shabbiest uniform and epaulets, leaving newest behind under wife's (or it might be his widow's) guardianship. This famous dandy of Windsor and Hyde Park went off on campaign with kit as modest as that of sergeant, and with something like prayer on his lips for woman he was leaving. Took her up from ground, held her in his arms for minute, tight pressed against strong-beating heart. Face was purple and eyes dim as he put her down and left her. Rode by his General's side, smoked cigar in silence as they hastened after troops of General's brigade, which preceded them; not until some miles on their way that he left off twirling moustache and broke silence.**
- **Earlier Status**: Secretly married to Rebecca; heavily indebted. Extracted considerable payment from George in bank-notes and bill on agents; lost £140 to George at cards. Met Miss Crawley when she took air in chair; she held out couple of fingers; Rawdon turned red as scarlet. Miss Crawley subsequently disparaged his appearance. **In Belgium**: Now in Brussels lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rebecca and General Tufto. Encountered Osborne party in park; shook hands heartily with Amelia and spoke warmly to Jos; stared at Mrs. O'Dowd's face and black cock's feathers until she thought she made conquest. Sent message to George at opera inviting him to dinner Tuesday when General dines out; asked George to "make Sedley cut off his moustache." Said "Hm, as you please" when George expressed intention to pay respects to Rebecca alone, looking very glum; two young officers exchanged knowing glances. Repeatedly together with George now; George always welcome in quarters. **Lets Osborne come and go with entire good humour; understood perfectly well with Rebecca (though never absolutely conspired in so many words) that one cajoled young gentleman whilst other won his money at cards; understood winning money from Osborne while flattering himself wife dying of love for him.**

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Departure Actions**: Wisely determined not to give way to unavailing sentimentality on Rawdon's departure. Waved him adieu from window, stood there moment looking out after he was gone. Cathedral towers and full gables of quaint old houses were just beginning to blush in sunrise. Had been no rest for her that night. Still in her pretty ball-dress, fair hair hanging somewhat out of curl on her neck, circles round her eyes dark with watching. "What a fright I seem," she said, examining herself in glass, "and how pale this pink makes one look!" Divested herself of pink raiment; in doing which note fell out from her corsage, which she picked up with smile and locked into dressing-box. Put bouquet of ball into glass of water and went to bed and slept very comfortably. **Found in Rawdon's pocket-book draft for twenty pounds on Osborne's banker. This made her think about Mrs. Osborne. "I will go and get the draft cashed," she said, "and pay a visit afterwards to poor little Emmy." Passed morning disposing, ordering, looking out, and locking up her properties in most agreeable manner. Made calculations of Rawdon's valuables; found with pungent feeling of triumph and self-satisfaction that should circumstances occur, she might reckon on six or seven hundred pounds at very least, to begin world with. Narrator remarks: "If this is a novel without a hero, at least let us lay claim to a heroine. No man in the British army which has marched away, not the great Duke himself, could be more cool or collected in the presence of doubts and difficulties, than the indomitable little aide-de-camp's wife."**
- **Earlier Status**: Secretly married to Rawdon; heavily indebted. Successfully reconciled with Miss Briggs on beach. Sent crumpled note to Rawdon requesting money from "Cupid" (George); Rawdon extracted considerable payment; remarked "comfortable inn in Brighton is better than spunging-house in Chancery Lane." Packed chief valuables sent to London under care of George's servant. **In Belgium**: Now in Brussels with Rawdon and General Tufto at Hotel du Parc. Encountered Osborne party in Park riding on beautiful little Arab in prettiest tightest riding-habit (acquired art at Queen's Crawley); accompanied by General Tufto amid greatest persons in Brussels. Acknowledged Amelia graciously with nod, smile, playful finger-kissing. At opera: performed hand-kissing toward Amelia's box; clapped hands when George entered her box; General Tufto's presence noted—he stared at George with sulky scowl. Rebecca left box leaning on Dobbin's arm. During her time in Amelia's box, bustled, chattered, turned and twisted, smiled upon one, smirked on another; admired Mrs. O'Dowd's Cairngorm brooch and Irish diamonds. After opera, General Tufto cursed "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; was jealous and angry. Osborne and Crawley repeatedly together now; George always welcome in their apartments. When Amelia and George visited, Amelia displayed evident unwillingness; nearly caused first quarrel; George scolded Amelia violently; Amelia bashful and awkward on second visit. Rebecca remarked to George: thought Amelia jealous at Brighton; now supposes scandalized because Rawdon, Rebecca, and General live together; questioned how they could live without friend to share expenses; claimed she was "very much obliged to Emmy, very"; revealed General ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours"; pert toss of head; invited George to dinner; General dines with Commander-in-Chief. **At Brussels ball: invited; danced with George twice or thrice; made request to George for scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days). Later at hotel after ball: Rebecca and Rawdon discussed financial schemes—Rebecca saying "we have not done with your aunt yet; if she fails us, isn't there what you call the Gazette? or when your uncle Bute's life drops, I have another scheme. Living has always belonged to younger brother, why shouldn't you sell out and go into the Church?" Idea of conversion set Rawdon into roars of laughter (explosion heard through hotel at midnight); General Tufto heard haw-haws of great dragoon's voice from quarters on first floor above them; Rebecca acted scene with great spirit and preached Rawdon's first sermon to immense delight of General at breakfast.**

**Jos Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Departure Morning**: **Non-combatant left behind. Rest broken like other people's by sounding of bugles in early morning. Being great sleeper fond of his bed, might have snoozed on until usual hour of rising despite all drums, bugles, and bagpipes, but was roused by Captain Dobbin (not George, who occupied with own affairs and grief at parting with wife, too much to think of taking leave of slumbering brother-in-law). Dobbin insisted on shaking hands before departure; instructed Jos to watch over Amelia, comfort her, see no harm comes to her; if anything happens to George, she has no one but Jos to look to; if goes wrong with army, Jos will see her safe back to England; Jos must promise never to desert her; asked if Jos needs gold to return to England in case of misfortune.**
- **Earlier Status**: Arrived Chatham in fine carriage with Amelia; recognized Dobbin; attended Mrs. O'Dowd's party in maudlin state; told tiger-hunt story. Agreed to escort Amelia and Mrs. O'Dowd abroad; ceased shaving upper lip; followed parades and drills with great assiduity; received excellent assistance from Mrs. O'Dowd in military studies. Made appearance in braided frock-coat and duck trousers, foraging cap with smart gold band. **In Belgium**: Interposed about curry and rice; owned with sigh that England had no equal for good streaky beef despite Mrs. O'Dowd's assertions. Hired pair of horses for open carriage in Brussels; made tolerable figure in drives about Park. Accompanied Amelia on carriage drives; more at ease when great man (General Tufto with Rebecca) departed. Referenced Battle of Salamanca. At opera: eating ice; Rebecca admired Jos with "kindliest greeting." **At Brussels ball: panting to be asked with Mrs. O'Dowd; strove in vain to procure tickets; made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation.**

**Mrs. Major Peggy O'Dowd** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- One of five sisters and eleven children of Glenmalony. **Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, became very grave. Major told her to wake him half an hour before assembly beats, call him at half-past one, prepare his things; may be he'll not come back to breakfast (signifying regiment will march next morning). After regiment's departure, betook herself to large volume of uncle the Dean's sermons for meditation; perhaps did not understand much; thoughts were elsewhere; sleep project with poor Mick's nightcap on pillow was quite vain one. She who remains and suffers—has leisure to think, brood, remember.**
- In Brussels: continually prattles about Ballinasloe, Dublin cattle, markets, Glenmalony. Cock's plume in hat and large repeater on stomach. **Not invited to Brussels ball; panted to be asked; strove in vain to procure tickets; made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation. At opera: wore splendid Irish diamonds and Cairngorms; tossed about fan with splendid complacency; when Rebecca performed hand-kissing, Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment to herself and returned gracious smile, sending Dobbin shrieking from box. Rebecca admired her brooch and diamonds, wouldn't believe they were not from Golconda direct. Made timely observation when neither lady rallied ("Why didn't you BOY one?" regarding bouquets); became silent and subdued afterward.**

**Major Mick O'Dowd** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Served sovereign in every quarter of world; paid for every step by acts of daring and gallantry. Most modest, silent, sheep-faced, meek of little men; obedient to wife. **Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, placidly pulled nightcap over his ears, told Peggy: "that there will be such a ball danced in a day or two as some of 'em has never heard the chune of"; much more happy to retire to rest after quiet tumbler than figure at other sort of amusement. Asked to be woken half an hour before assembly beats, called at half-past one, things ready; may be he'll not come back to breakfast; words signified opinion that regiment would march next morning; ceased talking and fell asleep.**

**John Osborne (Old Mr. Osborne)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Wealthy merchant; George's father; savage, determined man. Upon learning George married Amelia, erupted in fury. Locked himself in study; retrieved mahogany escritoire; examined George's documents with "curses quivering on livid lips" and "horrid hatred and disappointment"; marked, docketed, catalogued with dates. Commissioned lawyer to draft letter stating determination "final and irrevocable." George ceases to be family member. News how son is entertaining peers and peeresses came to Osborne's ears in the City. **George wrote farewell letter to him at dawn before regiment's departure, remembering his past generosity and thousand kindnesses, sealed and kissed superscription.**

**General Tufto** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Military officer in Brussels with considerable status. Lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rawdon and Rebecca. Dines out almost constantly; Tuesday mentioned as occasion dining with Commander-in-Chief. **At opera: stared at George with sulky scowl when George entered Rebecca's box; disengaged eye working round in Rebecca's direction, shooting out bloodshot glances at her and George; when Rebecca left box with George, gave low utterance to curses "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; curses came from heart; was jealous and angry; ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours" (Amelia). Capable of generating such lust and fury, rage and hatred. Heard roars of laughter from Rawdon and Rawdon's haw-haws through hotel at midnight (Rebecca's Church conversion scene preached to him at breakfast, to immense delight).**

## Critical Facts and Status

**WATERLOO CAMPAIGN - BATTLE COMMENCES**: **French have crossed Sambre; British left already engaged. Regiment receives marching orders in early morning hours—marches within quarter hour. Bugle from Place of Arms signals at dawn; whole city awakens to drums and pipes. Major O'Dowd indicates regiment will march; asks to be woken at half-past one. After regiment's departure, Amelia left at bedside as George departed with troops.**

**GEORGE-AMELIA MARRIAGE - SEVERED AT CRITICAL MOMENT**: Married late April; disinherited "final and irrevocable"; receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Not quite six weeks married. **George carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she not deceived); consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." Amelia aware but does not plague him with jealousy; becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. Does not know Amelia is not suspicious (all acquaintance perfectly aware). At Brussels ball: George left Amelia unnoticed on bench; danced with Rebecca twice or thrice; came at Rebecca's request for scarf and flowers twenty times in last few days. Amelia found this "quite too much"; clung to Dobbin, called him by Christian name, begged him to take her home; did not sleep that night. Nearly had first quarrel over Amelia's unwillingness to visit Rebecca; George scolded her violently; she silent but bashful and awkward on second visit. At final moment before departure: George bent over Amelia's bedside; she awoke and threw her fair arms round his neck with sob, saying "I am awake, George"; bugle sounded, city awoke; George departed with regiment.**

**DOBBIN'S FINAL CHARGE**: Before departure, came to Jos's quarters and roused him from sleep. Commanded Jos to stay in Brussels and watch over Amelia; comfort her; see no harm comes to her; if anything happens to George, she has no one in world to look to; if goes wrong with army, Jos will see her safe back to England; Jos must promise on word never to desert her. Asked if Jos needs gold to return to England. (Dobbin appeared hypocrite, listening intently toward George's apartments, striding about, upsetting chairs, beating tattoo, biting nails—showing great inward emotion—while professing tender interest in Jos.)

**REBECCA'S CUNNING AND CALCULATION**: Upon Rawdon's departure, wisely determined not to give way to sentimentality. Waved him adieu from window and went to bed and slept comfortably while still wearing ball-dress with dark circles under eyes from watching all night. Found draft for twenty pounds on Osborne's banker in Rawdon's pocket-book; determined to get it cashed and visit "poor little Emmy." Made calculations of Rawdon's valuables; found she might reckon on six or seven hundred pounds at very least to begin world with. Passed morning disposing, ordering, looking out, and locking up her properties in most agreeable manner. Narrator marks her as "indomitable little aide-de-camp's wife"—as cool and collected as great Duke himself in presence of doubts and difficulties.

**RAWDON'S GENUINE CONCERN**: Upon final news of campaign, showed genuine gravity for first time; expressed concern about providing for those he brought into scrape; dressed in oldest and shabbiest uniform, leaving newest behind for Rebecca's widow's needs; made list of possessions that might be sold for her benefit; held her in his arms tight pressed against strong-beating heart before departure, face purple and eyes dim; left her silently.
